claims.text: Broadening the mixture of first-row transition metals increases the configurational disorder of the high-entropy spinel oxide support.
Increased configurational disorder generates a defect-rich spinel lattice.
Increased configurational disorder raises the concentration of oxygen vacancies.
Oxygen vacancies and defect-rich surfaces enhance oxygen activation.
Defect-rich surfaces provide anchoring sites for Pt atoms.
An optimized Pt deposition protocol incorporating a stabilizing agent can produce atomically dispersed Pt.
Stabilized atomic Pt dispersion and the disordered support synergistically modulate the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Modulation of intermediate binding energies improves catalytic kinetics.
Atomic Pt anchoring and stabilized dispersion mitigate Pt sintering during prolonged high-temperature operation.
The intervention will reduce the oxidation T10 by approximately 50–60% relative to conventional Pt/carbon catalysts.
The intervention will improve durability under automotive exhaust cycling relative to conventional Pt/carbon catalysts.
The proposed catalyst can achieve the predicted activity and durability while using a lower Pt loading than the baseline.
The high-entropy spinel support is an M3O4-type oxide composed of first-row transition metals and prepared by solventless thermolysis.
The proposed support can be synthesized by solventless thermolysis at approximately 500 °C in air.
The hypothesized behavior should hold during simulated exhaust testing between 250 and 600 °C with fluctuating gas compositions.
Temperatures outside the specified range or drastic changes in gas composition may alter catalyst behavior.
The long-term stability of the modified Pt/support structure under extended high-temperature cycling is uncertain.
